fields.Front: Why organize networks in layers? Give the two benefits from the slides.
fields.Back:
Networks have many pieces (hosts, routers, links, applications, protocols, hardware, software).
1) Explicit structure lets us identify the pieces and their relationships: a layered reference model for discussion.
2) Modularization eases maintenance and updating: a change in one layer's service implementation is transparent to the rest (changing the gate procedure does not affect ticketing).

fields.Front: In the air-travel analogy, what are the five layers (services), and what does each layer's implementation rely on?
fields.Back:
Ticketing service (purchase / complain), baggage service (check / claim), gate service (load / unload), runway service (takeoff / landing), airplane routing service.
Each layer implements its service via its own internal-layer actions and by relying on the services of the layer below (gates use runway-to-runway transfer).

fields.Front: In what sense might layering be 'considered harmful'? Give two drawbacks.
fields.Back:
1) Duplicated functionality: e.g., error recovery done both per link (link layer) and end to end (transport).
2) A layer may need information that lives only in another layer, breaking the separation.
In practice the benefits of modular structure win.

fields.Front: List the five layers of the Internet protocol stack top to bottom, with one protocol and the PDU name for each.
fields.Back:
1) Application: HTTP, SMTP, IMAP (DNS); message.
2) Transport: TCP, UDP; segment.
3) Network: IP, routing protocols; datagram.
4) Link: Ethernet, 802.11 WiFi, PPP; frame.
5) Physical: medium-specific bit signalling; bit.

fields.Front: Application layer: role, example protocols, PDU, and where it is implemented.
fields.Back:
Role: supports network applications (Web documents, email, name lookup).
Protocols: HTTP, SMTP, IMAP, DNS.
PDU: message.
Implemented in software on hosts only (not in routers).

fields.Front: Transport layer: role, its two protocols and how they differ, PDU, and where implemented.
fields.Back:
Role: process-to-process data transfer between application endpoints.
TCP: connection-oriented, reliable delivery, flow control, congestion control. UDP: connectionless, no-frills, none of those.
PDU: segment.
Implemented in software on hosts only.

fields.Front: Network layer: role, protocols, PDU, and where implemented.
fields.Back:
Role: routing of datagrams from source host to destination host.
Protocols: IP (the one protocol every network-layer component must run; the layer is often called 'the IP layer') plus routing protocols that compute paths.
PDU: datagram.
Implemented in hosts and routers.

fields.Front: Link layer and physical layer: role of each, example protocols, PDU, where implemented, and how link-layer reliability differs from TCP's.
fields.Back:
Link layer: data transfer between neighbouring network elements (one hop); a datagram may cross different link protocols on different hops (WiFi on one, Ethernet on the next). Protocols: Ethernet, 802.11 (WiFi), PPP, DOCSIS. PDU: frame.
Physical layer: moves the individual bits within a frame from one node to the next; the protocol depends on the medium (twisted pair, coax, fiber, radio). PDU: bit.
Both are implemented in the network interface card. Link-layer reliability covers one link; TCP reliability is end to end.

fields.Front: Sort these into layers: TCP, IP, HTTP, Ethernet, UDP, SMTP, 802.11, PPP, IMAP, DNS.
fields.Back:
Application: HTTP, SMTP, IMAP, DNS.
Transport: TCP, UDP.
Network: IP.
Link: Ethernet, 802.11 (WiFi), PPP.

fields.Front: Compare the ISO/OSI reference model with the Internet's 5-layer stack: how many layers, which two are extra, what they do, and how the Internet handles them.
fields.Back:
OSI (late 1970s) has 7 layers; the Internet stack has 5.
Extra layers sit between application and transport: presentation (data interpretation: encryption, compression, machine-specific conventions) and session (delimiting and synchronizing exchanges, checkpointing, recovery).
The Internet leaves these services to the application developer.
OSI numbering survives as jargon: 'layer 2 switch', 'layer 3 router'.

fields.Text: Each layer implements a service via its own {{c1::internal-layer actions}} and by relying on the services provided by the {{c1::layer below}}; a change in a layer's service {{c1::implementation}} is transparent to the rest of the system.
Internet protocol stack, top to bottom: {{c1::application}}, {{c1::transport}}, {{c1::network}}, {{c1::link}}, {{c1::physical}}.
PDU names: application = {{c1::message}}, transport = {{c1::segment}}, network = {{c1::datagram}}, link = {{c1::frame}}, physical = {{c1::bit}}.
Example protocols per layer: application {{c1::HTTP, SMTP, IMAP}}; transport {{c1::TCP, UDP}}; network {{c1::IP, routing protocols}}; link {{c1::Ethernet, 802.11 (WiFi), PPP}}.

OSI 7-layer model top to bottom: application, {{c1::presentation}}, {{c1::session}}, transport, network, {{c1::data link}}, physical; a 'layer {{c1::2}}' device is a switch and a 'layer {{c1::3}}' device is a router.
